scenes.tts: Potassium has far more conductance than sodium. So why doesn't the cell rest right at potassium's mark?
scenes.visual: The voltage scale from chapter 1: E_K = −95 mV left, E_Na = +60.6 mV right, marker at −71.2 mV. The question appears above it.
scenes.narration: Potassium has far more conductance than sodium. So why doesn't the cell rest right at potassium's mark?

scenes.tts: Back to the scale. Potassium's rope is thick. Sodium's rope is thin.
scenes.visual: The purple rope thick, the orange rope thin. On screen only: g_K = 8.47 nS, g_Na = 1.53 nS.
scenes.narration: Back to the scale. Potassium's rope is thick. Sodium's rope is thin.

scenes.tts: The marker slides until the two pulls are equal and opposite. That spot is the balance point.
scenes.visual: The marker starts at 0 mV, slides left, and stops where two pull arrows of equal width meet. A ghost label: balance point.
scenes.narration: The marker slides until the two pulls are equal and opposite. That spot is the balance point.

scenes.tts: Which end does the marker settle nearer? And roughly how far along?
scenes.visual: On screen: Pause. Thick purple rope, thin orange rope. Which end, and how far along?
scenes.narration: Which end does the marker settle nearer? And roughly how far along?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: Nearer potassium. The pulls are equal, so the thin rope must be stretched farther.
scenes.visual: The orange rope is drawn long and taut; the purple rope short. Arrows of equal width.
scenes.narration: Nearer potassium. The pulls are equal, so the thin rope must be stretched farther.

scenes.tts: Potassium's rope is about five and a half times stronger. So the marker sits about five and a half times closer to its mark.
scenes.visual: On screen only: 8.47 / 1.53 ≈ 5.5. The 155.6 mV gap splits into 23.8 mV (to E_K) and 131.8 mV (to E_Na).
scenes.narration: Potassium's rope is about five and a half times stronger. So the marker sits about five and a half times closer to its mark.

scenes.tts: That puts rest at about minus seventy-one millivolts. And the two gaps are the sizes of the driving forces from before.
scenes.caption: That puts rest at about −71 mV. And the two gaps are the sizes of the driving forces from before.
scenes.visual: Marker at −71.2 mV. The gaps 23.8 and 131.8 mV are labelled driving-force sizes. Beside them, the signed values: Vm − E_K = +23.8 mV, Vm − E_Na = −131.8 mV, matching chapter 1.
scenes.narration: That puts rest at about −71 mV. And the two gaps are the sizes of the driving forces from before.

scenes.tts: The algebra says the same thing. Set the currents to add up to zero, and solve for the voltage.
scenes.visual: On screen, line by line: g_K (Vm − E_K) + g_Na (Vm − E_Na) = 0; Vm (g_K + g_Na) = g_K E_K + g_Na E_Na.
scenes.narration: The algebra says the same thing. Set the currents to add up to zero, and solve for the voltage.

scenes.tts: The resting potential comes out as an average of the equilibrium potentials.
scenes.visual: Third line appears, boxed: Vm = (g_K E_K + g_Na E_Na) / (g_K + g_Na). On screen only: (8.47 × −95 + 1.53 × 60.6) / 10 = −71.2 mV.
scenes.narration: The resting potential comes out as an average of the equilibrium potentials.

scenes.tts: Each one is weighted by its conductance. More ions just add more terms, above and below the line.
scenes.visual: Each g in the box glows in its rope's colour. A grey third term fades in above and below the line, then fades out.
scenes.narration: Each one is weighted by its conductance. More ions just add more terms, above and below the line.

scenes.tts: Do not shorten this to a rule about the biggest conductance. With three or more conductances, that shortcut can fail.
scenes.visual: A crossed-out card: rest sits nearest the biggest conductance. Beside it: use the weighted average.
scenes.narration: Do not shorten this to a rule about the biggest conductance. With three or more conductances, that shortcut can fail.

scenes.tts: Three consequences follow. Open more of one ion's channels, and the balance point slides toward that ion's mark.
scenes.visual: Card 1 of 3. The orange rope thickens; the marker slides right.
scenes.narration: Three consequences follow. Open more of one ion's channels, and the balance point slides toward that ion's mark.

scenes.tts: Close some, and it slides away.
scenes.visual: Card 2 of 3. The orange rope thins back; the marker slides left.
scenes.narration: Close some, and it slides away.

scenes.tts: Scale every leak up together, and the passive balance point stays put. But something else changes, as later chapters show.
scenes.visual: Card 3 of 3. Both ropes thicken together; the marker does not move. Small label: no injected current; pump's direct current omitted. A small flag: something else changes.
scenes.narration: Scale every leak up together, and the passive balance point stays put. But something else changes, as later chapters show.

scenes.tts: Double the sodium conductance, and rest moves toward sodium. But only partway, because potassium's rope is still stronger.
scenes.visual: The orange rope doubles in thickness. The marker slides right and stops well short of 0 mV, still nearer E_K. On screen only: g_Na 1.53 → 3.06 nS; (8.47 × −95 + 3.06 × 60.6) / 11.53 ≈ −53.7 mV.
scenes.narration: Double the sodium conductance, and rest moves toward sodium. But only partway, because potassium's rope is still stronger.

scenes.tts: Keep one number from this cell: its total leak, ten nanosiemens. It comes back in the next chapter.
scenes.caption: Keep one number from this cell: its total leak, 10 nS. It comes back in the next chapter.
scenes.visual: A tag pinned to the corner of the screen: total leak g_K + g_Na = 10 nS.
scenes.narration: Keep one number from this cell: its total leak, 10 nS. It comes back in the next chapter.

scenes.tts: Often you know concentrations and permeabilities, not conductances. Then you calculate with the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation.
scenes.visual: The GHK voltage equation fades in as a caption box: Vm = (RT/F) ln[(P_K[K]o + P_Na[Na]o + P_Cl[Cl]i) / (P_K[K]i + P_Na[Na]i + P_Cl[Cl]o)].
scenes.narration: Often you know concentrations and permeabilities, not conductances. Then you calculate with the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation.

scenes.tts: It writes the same zero net current condition in those terms. Each ion counts in proportion to its permeability.
scenes.visual: The potassium terms top and bottom glow purple, the sodium terms orange. Label: same balance, written in permeabilities.
scenes.narration: It writes the same zero net current condition in those terms. Each ion counts in proportion to its permeability.

scenes.tts: For our cell, it gives the same rest, about minus seventy-one millivolts.
scenes.caption: For our cell, it gives the same rest, about −71 mV.
scenes.visual: On screen only: P_K = 1, P_Na = 0.04, P_Cl = 0; top 9.8 mM, bottom 140.6 mM; Vm = 26.72 × ln(9.8/140.6) = −71.2 mV.
scenes.narration: For our cell, it gives the same rest, about −71 mV.

scenes.tts: Permeability and conductance are different measures of the same channels.
scenes.visual: Two labels side by side: permeability ratio 1 : 0.04; conductance ratio 8.47 : 1.53 (about 1 : 0.18). A bracket joins them: same cell.
scenes.narration: Permeability and conductance are different measures of the same channels.

scenes.tts: Permeability describes the pathway. Conductance here is the current divided by its driving force, the gap between the voltage and the ion's equilibrium potential. It also depends on the ions on each side, and the voltage.
scenes.visual: Under permeability: property of the pathway. Under conductance: chord conductance = I / (Vm − E_ion); depends on ion numbers on each side and on voltage.
scenes.narration: Permeability describes the pathway. Conductance here is the current divided by its driving force, the gap between the voltage and the ion's equilibrium potential. It also depends on the ions on each side, and the voltage.

scenes.tts: So reason with the balance point. Calculate with the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation when you have concentrations and permeabilities.
scenes.visual: Card: Reason with the balance point (which way, and why). Calculate with GHK (given concentrations and permeabilities).
scenes.narration: So reason with the balance point. Calculate with the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation when you have concentrations and permeabilities.

scenes.tts: One more piece. Left alone, these leaks would run the gradients down.
scenes.visual: The cell returns. K+ dots stream out and Na+ dots in; the inside and outside shading slowly evens out.
scenes.narration: One more piece. Left alone, these leaks would run the gradients down.

scenes.tts: The sodium-potassium pump puts the ions back. Three sodium go out and two potassium come in, for each ATP.
scenes.visual: A small pump in the membrane cycles: three orange dots out, two purple dots in. The shading restores. Label: Na+/K+ pump, 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP.
scenes.narration: The sodium-potassium pump puts the ions back. Three sodium go out and two potassium come in, for each ATP.

scenes.tts: So rest is a steady state, kept up by the pump. It is not an equilibrium. The pump's own current can also shift rest a little more negative. In many cells that shift is small, but it varies.
scenes.visual: Card: rest = steady state (kept up by the pump), not equilibrium. Small note: the pump's own outward current adds a direct hyperpolarization, small in many cells but variable.
scenes.narration: So rest is a steady state, kept up by the pump. It is not an equilibrium. The pump's own current can also shift rest a little more negative. In many cells that shift is small, but it varies.

scenes.tts: With no current injected, and the pump's own current set aside, rest is where the leaks balance: the conductance-weighted average of the reversal potentials.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: with no injected current and the pump's direct current omitted, rest = the passive balance point, the conductance-weighted average of E_K and E_Na.
scenes.narration: With no current injected, and the pump's own current set aside, rest is where the leaks balance: the conductance-weighted average of the reversal potentials.
